one_liner: Rust columnar file format and compressed-array toolkit that aims to replace Parquet for scans, writes and random access.
what_it_does: Vortex is an on-disk columnar file format plus an in-memory array library. You write a stream of Arrow-compatible arrays; the writer picks per-chunk encodings, builds zone-map statistics and serializes a layout tree with a flatbuffer footer. Reads go through a Scan API with filter and projection pushdown that returns independently executable splits. You can use it from Rust, Python (vortex-data), Java/Spark, a C API and a C++20 wrapper, or from DuckDB (INSTALL vortex) and DataFusion. It is not a Parquet drop-in: you have to convert existing data first (for example with DuckDB COPY ... (FORMAT vortex)), and every reader needs Vortex support.
how_it_is_fast: Each chunk gets its own chain of lightweight encodings, chosen by a BtrBlocks-style sampling compressor. Integers use FastLanes SIMD bit-packing, frame-of-reference, delta and RLE; floats use ALP/ALPrd; strings use FSST. Dictionary, run-end and sparse encodings apply across types, and zstd/PCodec are kept for the size-oriented 'compact' strategy. Arrays are lazy trees of encodings, so filters, takes and comparisons run directly on compressed data when a kernel exists, and data is fully decoded only when no kernel does. The DuckDB integration can hand FSST strings to DuckDB without decompressing them. The default file layout keeps min/max/null-count zone maps every 8k rows for pruning and targets segments of about 1 MB, a size chosen for S3 request sizing. The writer compresses chunks in parallel across all available cores, and footer metadata is zero-copy and zero-parse.
when_to_use: Write-once, scan-many analytics tables that you query through DuckDB or DataFusion on local NVMe. On the dashboard, TPC-H SF1 on NVMe takes 450 ms with DuckDB+Vortex vs 1.51 s with DuckDB+Parquet.

Point lookups and sparse row fetches (take) over columnar data such as feature vectors, taxi trips or nested lists/structs, where Parquet's lack of row-level random access hurts. Hot take is 1.85 ms vs 65 s for Parquet and 3.57 ms for Lance.
Rust data systems or custom storage engines that want Arrow-compatible arrays with compressed-domain compute, plus pluggable encodings, layouts and storage backends (local disk, object stores).
Bulk ingest or conversion on many-core machines, where the parallel writer can use every core. The dashboard shows 1,756 MB/s vs 605 MB/s for parquet-rs, with the threading caveat below.
GPU decode pipelines on Linux, using the optional CUDA feature that decodes Vortex files on the device.
when_not_to_use: As an interchange format for arbitrary consumers. Parquet is readable almost everywhere, while Vortex needs its own library or extension. Iceberg support is still 'coming soon', and DuckDB extension updates need DuckDB maintainers to redeploy, so they can lag Vortex releases by days.

Large queries over S3 with DuckDB. On the same dashboard, TPC-H S3 SF100 takes 488.6 s with DuckDB+Vortex vs 73.5 s with DuckDB+Parquet, and at S3 SF1 DataFusion+Parquet is fastest. Independent ClickBench runs are mixed to negative (DataFusion+Vortex 91.3 s vs 45.6 s for Parquet, Aug 2026). The project's own epic #7716 lists ClickBench, TPC-H and TPC-DS queries where it still loses to Parquet.

Memory-constrained ingest through DuckDB. In #10046, COPY ... (FORMAT vortex) of ClickBench hits was OOM-killed on a 7.6 GiB host regardless of memory_limit, because Vortex allocations are invisible to DuckDB's accounting. The C, C++ and DuckDB write paths are effectively single-threaded (#8760). An independent May 2026 test also hit OOM reading directories of Vortex files through the DuckDB extension.
Many small writes. In #5861, writing RecordBatches under about 1,000 rows was 20-30x slower than Parquet, although that test used uncompressed Parquet.

When smallest file size is the goal. The dashboard's geomean Vortex file size is 1.07x Parquet-zstd (range 0.55x to 1.43x); the 'compact' strategy trades read speed for size. Also, the Rust and C++ APIs still change between 0.x releases, and the Scan API is marked as under development.

integration.form: crate (vortex on crates.io). Also a PyPI module (vortex-data), a Maven Spark package, a DuckDB extension, and C/C++ libraries built from source with CMake as static or shared libs.
integration.dependencies: The workspace pins arrow-rs 59.x, flatbuffers, fastlanes, fsst-rs, zstd, pco, object_store and tokio. Engine integrations use DataFusion 55 or DuckDB 1.5. The C/C++ bindings need CMake 3.25+ and Cargo/rustc on PATH; nanoarrow provides optional Arrow interop. The README recommends mimalloc as the global allocator.
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.95 MSRV (edition 2024), with CI building on 1.98. The C++ bindings need a C++20 compiler and CMake 3.25+.
integration.platforms: Rust crate platforms are not documented. The C/C++ bindings build natively only on Linux x86-64/aarch64 and macOS arm64; Windows, musl, cross-compilation and universal binaries are unsupported. The CUDA path is Linux-only.
integration.thread_safety: Scans produce independent splits/partitions meant for parallel consumption, and arrays, dtypes and expressions are reference-counted and cheap to clone. The FFI runs on caller threads unless you set vx_runtime_set_worker_threads. Open bug #9817: a Vortex CurrentThreadRuntime driven inside tokio block_on can stall forever.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — it is Arrow-compatible in memory and plugs into DuckDB, DataFusion, Spark and Polars, but data must be converted from Parquet, there is no Parquet API compatibility, and every reader needs Vortex support.

gotchas: Backward compatibility covers only files written by 0.36.0 or later. The default session writes the newest frozen edition, so a library upgrade can produce files that older readers cannot open. Pin an edition when readers lag behind writers.

Open correctness bugs: #9205 (null children of a nullable struct leak into zone maps, so is_null filters can prune valid zones and return wrong results) and #9836 (sum overflow handled incorrectly in the DuckDB integration). Fuzzing has found panics on malformed files (#8848, #8823), so isolate untrusted inputs.
Memory: take on an FSST string array grew 19 MB into 2 GB (#4784), and buffer allocations bypass host-engine memory limits until the BufferAllocator work (#9674) lands.
C++ API: the Writer must call finish() or the file is corrupt. Literals need an explicit type, as in lit<uint16_t>(180), because there is no type coercion; a plain lit(180) fails at runtime.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Vortex over Lance for SQL analytics through DuckDB or DataFusion when file size matters. On Vortex's own dashboard, Lance files are 2.11x Parquet size vs 1.07x for Vortex, and Lance trails on write, scan and take (first-party numbers). Velox, StarRocks, Umbra and Sirius are query engines, not formats: Vortex sits underneath an engine such as DuckDB, DataFusion or Spark rather than replacing one.
verified_claims_summary: Vortex's own CI dashboard (bench.vortex.dev build 737386b; AWS c8gd.metal-24xl ARM64 per the workflows; rustc 1.98 with target-cpu=native) reports geomean write throughput of 1,756 vs 605 MB/s and scan throughput of 84.1 vs 3.2 GB/s against parquet-rs 59 with default ZSTD, plus hot take latency of 1.85 ms vs 65 s. These are not per-core comparisons: the Vortex side runs on a multi-threaded Tokio runtime with a writer that compresses on all cores, while the Parquet side uses parquet-rs's synchronous ArrowWriter and reader. End-to-end query gains are smaller and mixed: ClickBench on NVMe is 3.99 vs 6.08 s with DataFusion and 4.65 vs 5.45 s with DuckDB, TPC-H S3 SF100 is 6.7x slower with DuckDB, and independent ClickBench runs on c6a.4xlarge are mixed to negative.
status_note: Very active: commits land daily, 0.86.1 shipped on 2026-09-11, and 0.x releases come every two to three weeks. It is Apache-2.0 and an LF AI & Data incubation project; the file format has been stable since 0.36.0, but library APIs still change between releases.
